name: Yoloxochitl Mixtec
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress; 2 further works by the same author (or citing it for stress) agree.

tone_statements.citation: DiCanio, Christian, Joshua Benn & Rey Castillo García. 2021. Disentangling the effects of position and utterance-level declination on the production of complex tones in Yoloxóchitl Mixtec. Language and Speech 64(3): 515-557 (first online 20 July 2020). doi:10.1177/0023830920939132
tone_statements.quote: All Oto-Manguean languages are tonal (see DiCanio & Bennett, Forthcoming) and YM possesses a large tonal inventory consisting of nine tonemes: /4, 3, 2, 1, 42, 32, 13, 14, 24/ (DiCanio et al., 2014, 2018).8 All content roots in YM are minimally bimoraic, consisting of either two syllables with short vowels, CVCV, or one syllable with a long vowel, CVV. The TBU is the mora in YM and contour tones may freely occur on both moras in disyllabic or monosyllabic roots ... Tone has a high functional load in YM—in addition to its lexical function, it is used to mark verbal aspect, negation, and person.
tone_statements.locator: p. 521, sec. 2.5 Background: Yoloxóchitl Mixtec; footnote 8 (p. 553): 'Tone /4/ is high and /1/ is low.'
tone_statements.summary: Nine tonemes (4 level, 5 contour; Chao-style digits, 4 = high), mora as TBU, fixed root-final stress; only /4,3,1,13,14/ on root-initial mora. Acoustic study, 9 speakers; declination for /1/,/3/ only.

tone_statements.quote: YM has nine basic tones that can occur on a single mora: four level tones (written as superscript numbers from /1/ for the low tone through /4/ for the high tone); three rising tones (/13/, /14/, and /24/) and two falling tones (/32/ and /42/).⁸ Again there are significant distributional gaps. Tone /2/ is never found on the initial mora; /32/ and /42/ are only word final and occur in the absence of any contrast with /31/ and /41/, both of which are absent in YM tonal phonology. ... There are 23 tonal melodies on bimoraic lexical stems.

tone_statements.summary: Nine tones per mora incl. rising/falling; 23 lexical melodies on bimoraic stems; first person marked by a purely tonal enclitic =2; rare /143 132 342/ on a few words (fn. 8); example count is a floor.

tone_statements.quote: In addition to lexical tone, there is evidence for root-final, fixed stress in Yoloxóchitl Mixtec. Whereas five lexical tones surface on non-final syllables of roots, nine surface on root-final syllables. Root-final syllables are also consistently longer than non-final syllables (DiCanio et al., 2018). One of the interesting manifestations of stress in the language is the asymmetry in onset consonant duration. Onset consonants in final stressed syllables are longer than onset consonants in nonfinal, unstressed syllables. [...] Yoloxóchitl Mixtec possesses a complex lexical tone system consisting of nine distinct tones which are moraically-aligned [p. 4]. Fixed stress occurs in stem-final syllables in Yoloxóchitl Mixtec (DiCanio, Benn, & Castillo García, 2018; DiCanio et al., 2020). Obstruents in the onset of stem-final syllables are both phonetically longer and less likely to be voiced than obstruents that occur in non-final syllables, including word-initial position [p. 2]. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 50(3): 333-365. doi:10.1017/S0025100318000294 (published PDF from author site; Glottolog id 570550 lists it as 2019, 1-33)
tone_statements.quote: Like many Oto-Manguean languages, words in Yoloxóchitl Mixtec have stress in addition to lexical tone. [...] In Yoloxóchitl Mixtec, stress falls on the final syllable of the couplet (the lexical root), not on the penult. The main acoustic realization of stress is increased duration. Final vowels are approximately 30–50% longer than penultimate vowels in words produced in isolation (DiCanio, Amith & Castillo García 2012, DiCanio, Benn & Castillo García 2018). Moreover, there is a distributional asymmetry with respect to tone on roots, with far more tonal contrasts occurring on root-final than penultimate syllables (DiCanio, Amith & Castillo García 2014). These two factors suggest that root-final syllables are stressed compared to non-final syllables.
